extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters / patent attorneys / patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on drafting and structuring patent claim sets (independent and dependent claims), analysing claim dependency for validity and infringement, and adapting claim format across jurisdictions (EPO, USPTO, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent claim must state essential elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The independent claim will state the essential elements of the invention. Those essential elements are necessary for achieving the technical effect underlying the solution of the technical problem with which the application is concerned (the problem usually being derived from the description).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The independent claim should contain all essential elements explicitly described in the description as necessary for the essential functionality of the invention. To achieve the broadest possible protection, the essential elements will be stretched to their greatest reasonable extent, taking into account the essential functionality and prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate an inventive-step strategy for all claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For all of the claims (independent and dependent), some argument of – or a strategy for – inventive step should be formulated, for example being nonobvious, or giving rise to an unexpected advantage or effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting claims, consider how each claim (including dependent fallback claims) can be supported with arguments for inventive step/nonobviousness and how claimed features contribute to technical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims as more particular embodiments / fallback positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims will be concerned with more particular embodiments of the invention — that is, a more specific disclosure of the invention than that set out in the independent claim. Some dependent claims should be drafted as 'fallback positions' in case the independent claim is found during prosecution (or litigation) to be not novel or to lack inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In brainstorming, identify order of importance of elements (essential and nonessential) taking into account patentability, commercial settings and enforcement possibilities. Draft dependent claims to provide fallback scope if broader claims are defeated.

rubrics_metrics.name: One dependent claim per selected/added element (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, one dependent claim is drafted per selected or added element. But there are cases (such as in a Markush formula) in which several elements (such as chemical radical values) are selected simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dependent claim adding an element selected from among a group or further characterizing an element can depend from only those preceding claims that themselves provide an antecedent for that element. A dependent claim adding an extra element does not need an antecedent; it can depend from any preceding claims and may (but need not) have multiple dependency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dependency ordering (add elements in decreasing importance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting dependent chains, elements may be added successively in decreasing order of importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify an order of importance for elements and draft dependent claims adding selected values in that order (e.g., A > B > C), producing singular dependency chains when successive selected elements are added.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer singular dependency for successive selected elements
rubrics_metrics.description: So far, Claims 1–3 form a dependency chain with only singular dependency, as is recommended when successive selected elements are added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adding successive selected elements, use singular dependency to form clear fallback chains. Multiple dependency can be used for other purposes but may complicate conversion to jurisdictions that disallow it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple dependent claims: permitted/recommended per jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: When, in the following dependent claims, an extra element is added, writing the claim in multiple dependent form is strongly recommended for the EPO, for the reasons explained in section 3.3. The claim set in this example will be appropriate for the EPO and those patent offices that allow multiple dependencies from multiple dependent claims — something not permitted at the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple dependency in EPO-style sets to offer broader coverage. However, before entering USPTO national phase, deconstruct multiple dependencies into appropriate singular dependencies and prepare US-style claims; otherwise multiple dependencies will not be allowed at the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating a dependency pyramid (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependency pyramid (many multiple dependencies whose vertex is Claim 1) is not generally recommended, because it does not offer good fallback positions in the event that the vertex Claim 1 is found not to be novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware that multiple dependencies might be erased or transformed by another drafter into claims all depending from Claim 1, creating a pyramid. Structure dependencies to preserve useful fallback positions rather than centralize everything on a single vertex claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse dependency groups separately for validity and infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis starts by separating out the different dependency groups (or a dependency chain), each one being formed of a single independent claim and all the claims that depend from it. Each dependency group is then considered separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For validity (novelty/inventive step) and infringement assessments, treat each dependency group independently. Use diagrams of claim scopes vs prior art or accused embodiments to determine which claims are novel/valid or infringed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume invalidity/infringement results propagate across dependencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Care must be taken not to conclude (wrongly) that invalidity of an independent claim necessarily implies invalidity of all of the claims dependent from it — a relatively frequent mistake made by nonexperts. Similarly, care must be taken not to conclude (wrongly) that infringement of the independent claim implies infringement of all the claims dependent from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: if prior art falls within a dependent claim's scope but outside another dependent claim, some dependent claims may remain novel/valid. If an accused embodiment falls within a dependent claim, it may also fall within broader claims in the chain, but absence from an independent claim means dependent chain claims are not infringed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part test for literal infringement assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaration of infringement involves making two judgments: (i) that at least one prohibited act has been carried out; and (ii) that the 'accused embodiment' associated with that prohibited act falls within the scope of at least one valid claim of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume the prohibited act is proven; then compare accused embodiment features with claim elements to decide literal infringement. Use dependency/group analysis to simplify: if embodiment outside independent claim, then claims depending from it are not infringed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brainstorming objectives when starting claim drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: The drafting process typically starts with a brainstorming meeting between the patent drafter and the inventor(s), with the initial objectives of: identifying the invention(s); selecting a claim type for the first independent claim; and choosing a preamble at an appropriate level for the dependency group corresponding to the independent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform brainstorming taking into account specific embodiments, drawings, and the closest prior art. Prioritize elements by commercial importance and patentability to plan fallback claims and enforcement strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble choice and claim format selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an appropriate preamble (e.g., 'A writing device' or two-part format) and claim type (product, process, apparatus, use) for the first independent claim in view of prior art (e.g., 'a writing device having A11 and B11' being prior art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a two-part claim (EPO-style) or standard/usual format is advisable. Be mindful that examiners may request two-part format, and that some formulations (e.g., 'apparatus for carrying out the process') may be construed as merely suitable for a purpose in some jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft to permit jurisdictional adaptation (PCT amendments / US conversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the PCT international application enters national/regional phases, use the opportunity under the PCT for amending the claims to fit national requirements. Great care should be taken when drafting a claim set appropriate to the USPTO. If this task is not performed by the same person who drafted the PCT application, they should give specific instructions about the detail underlying the original claim set to a new drafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare sets of claims to be deconstructed or expanded (e.g., deconstruct EPO multiple-dependency claims into USPTO-acceptable singular dependencies). Consider producing separate US-claim variants (broad and narrow dependency chains) to cover intermediate scopes and avoid added-matter/added-claim problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control total number of claims to avoid excess fees
rubrics_metrics.description: When adapting claim sets, keep the total number of claims within reasonable limits (ideally no more than 20 in examples given) to avoid extra claim fees (e.g., EPO allows 15 without extra fee at time of writing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use steps to generate claims that cover broadest, narrowest, and intermediate scopes while watching claim count. The example shows converting an EPO set with multiple dependencies into about 20 US-claims to cover a wide range of scopes without excessive fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claim considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims for products defined in terms of a process of manufacture are allowable in some jurisdictions, provided the products as such fulfill patentability requirements. A product is not typically rendered novel merely because it is made by means of a new process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The burden of proving distinguishing product-by-process features lies with the applicant, who may need evidence of different properties. In many jurisdictions (e.g., EPO) product-by-process claims are construed as claims to the product itself and confer absolute protection to that product. Some jurisdictions (e.g., Japan) may treat such claims as indefinite or only allow them in special circumstances. Always check whether product-by-process is permissible and strategically appropriate for the client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method/process claim drafting considerations (order and 'for' language)
rubrics_metrics.description: In many jurisdictions, the steps in a method claim are presumed to occur in any order, unless otherwise stated. A preamble with 'for' (e.g., 'an apparatus for carrying out the process') may be construed as meaning merely an apparatus suitable for the process in some jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting method claims, be explicit if sequence matters. For apparatus or product claims with purposive language, recognize that suitability for a purpose may not impose the same limitations as a method step. Consider jurisdictional treatment of use claims (e.g., EPO treats 'use of X as insecticide' equivalent to a process claim; US requires drafting as a process claim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Markush groups and consider equivalents to broaden claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering an element defined by a term of a preferred embodiment, the patent drafter should think of broader terms and other elements that a person skilled in the art would consider technical equivalents. Sometimes, including alternative elements in a Markush group may help in drafting broader claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider broadening from structural to functional terminology where supported. Use Markush groups where appropriate (e.g., C1, C2, C3, C4) and assess support in the description for broader terms and equivalence between variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional tip: edit claims to remove unnecessary words
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you believe you have reasonably captured the essence of the invention, review and re-review the claim to see how many words you can remove from it while still preserving the essence of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Involving the inventor in this process can help conceptualize the invention more clearly. Consider whether adjectives or qualifiers (e.g., 'pivotal' mounting) are strictly necessary for claim completeness or can be omitted to broaden scope.
